edits.english: And Rava says: A sin offering that one slaughtered for a person who is not obligated to bring anything, i.e., he said that he is slaughtering it for the sake of a person who is not obligated at all, is unfit. Why? As there is no person among the Jewish people who is not obligated to bring an offering for violating a positive mitzva.

One who is not obligated in a positive mitzva - meaning, who has not violated a positive mitzva. And concerning a positive mitzva, it is appropriate to speak of a sin offering, as the Gemara will explain further on.

The reason given for this matter, that there is no Jew who is not obligated in a positive mitzva, raises a question: For even one obligated to bring a burnt offering brings his offering to atone for a positive mitzva, so why in this case is the sin offering fit? Rashi wrote (see below) that one obligated in a burnt offering who is discussed here is one who has already designated a burnt offering and is obligated to sacrifice it. In such a case, the positive mitzvot that he violated do not require atonement by the sin offering. (And see Tosafot, who suggested the opposite, that the discussion is about one who has not yet designated an offering, but has accepted upon himself a burnt offering by vow. And see Keren Ora.)

Indeed, several difficulties arise in this small discussion, both due to the repetition in Rava’s statements, and because of the subsequent discussion, and because of the logical inference (see Tosafot Tukh and Sefat Emet and others). And Tosafot cited a version (and later commentaries wrote that it seems this was also the version of the Rambam) according to which this case refers to a burnt offering and not a sin offering. And Sefat Emet wrote that according to this, the order of Rava’s statements here is proper, for initially it was stated in his name that a change of owner in a sin offering is considered a change when the other is obligated in a similar atonement. And then it was stated that for the same reason the law would be so for a burnt offering (which did not fulfill the owner’s obligation), when one slaughters it for the sake of one who is not obligated at all.

(A sin offering slaughtered) for one who is not obligated in anything, it is unfit - if we read in this statement 'a burnt offering', for regarding a burnt offering too, it is written 'to atone for him'. But if we read 'a sin offering' here, why do I need Rava's other statement (that a sin offering atones for those obligated in a positive mitzva), for we learn it from here.
